summary: For ages 9–11: learning to evaluate the evidence behind scientific claims — deciding which evidence is relevant to a claim, whether it supports or refutes the claim, and how strong it is (a single anecdote vs a large, repeated, controlled study). Learners separate the CLAIM from the EVIDENCE, distinguish among facts, reasoned judgement based on research findings, and speculation, and learn that evidence can tip against a prior belief. The centrepiece activity is a weighing/sorting task with evidence cards; a role-play debate and sorting/ranking/competing-claims checks are retained as complementary approaches.
misconceptions: Assuming evidence can only support (confirm) an idea, not refute it — and defending a prior belief against contrary data (confirmation bias).
Treating all evidence as equally strong — giving a single anecdote the same weight as a large repeated study.
Confusing relevance with strength, or counting irrelevant-but-vivid information as evidence.
Mistaking assertion or opinion for evidence (not distinguishing fact from speculation).
Believing more evidence always wins, regardless of its quality or whether it actually bears on the claim.

activities.title: Weigh the evidence on a claim-balance
steps: Take a concrete claim, e.g. 'chewing gum improves memory' or 'this plant food makes seeds sprout faster', written at the top of a balance scale (drawn on paper or shown on screen).
Receive a deck of evidence cards: a friend's story (anecdote), a single quick test, a large repeated controlled study, and a couple of irrelevant-but-flashy facts.
Sort each card onto a 'supports / refutes / irrelevant' board, then place supporting and refuting cards on the balance so the scale tips for or against the claim.
Assign each card a strength and justify the placement using a strength ladder: anecdote / single reading < small controlled test < large, repeated, controlled study.
State a final judgement: which way does the evidence tip, and is it strong enough to accept, reject, or stay unsure about the claim?

OPTIONAL interactive version: drag cards onto the board and watch the scale physically tip, with each card's strength weighting the balance, irrelevant cards visibly doing nothing, and a filter that greys out non-evidence assertions.
activities.insight: In science it is the STRENGTH and RELEVANCE of evidence that decides an argument — not simply how many weak cards you pile on, nor how vivid the story is (although several strong, independent studies that agree do add weight). Sometimes the evidence tips the scale AGAINST the claim you started out believing.

activities.title: Debate the claim out loud
steps: Take a side in a spoken exchange where a partner (another learner, a teacher in role, or a scripted persona) advances a claim backed by weak evidence — e.g. a single anecdote.
Refute it with stronger evidence, naming why your evidence is stronger (controlled comparison, repeated trials).
Defend your own claim when the partner challenges it, and judge the quality of the evidence the partner offers rather than how confidently they speak.
Reach a reasoned position, revising it if the opponent's evidence turns out stronger.
activities.insight: Argument from evidence is a real exchange: you marshal evidence to support or refute, weigh an opponent's evidence by its design, and change your mind when the stronger evidence demands it.

activities.title: Sort, rank, and compare evidence across claims
steps: Categorise a set of evidence items for a given claim as supports / refutes / irrelevant.
Sequence several pieces of evidence from weakest to strongest and explain the ordering.
Given a mix of statements, sort them into three kinds — a fact/observation, a reasoned judgement based on research findings, and a speculation or bare opinion — and say how you can tell them apart.

Given two competing claims and a shared pool of evidence, decide for each piece which claim it supports, which it refutes, or whether it is irrelevant to both — then judge which claim the pool overall better supports.

As a quick warm-up, compare two short investigations and say whose evidence is stronger (controlled comparison with many trials vs a single uncontrolled observation); the full claim-vs-evidence reasoning is developed in the seed-sprouting check, so treat this as a brief classification, not a repeat of it.
activities.insight: Support-vs-refute, relevance, strength ranking, and telling facts from reasoned judgement and from speculation are separable judgements you can apply item by item — and the same evidence pool can bear differently on competing claims.

activities.title: Claim-versus-evidence check (seed sprouting)
steps: Read two accounts: Aisha says 'It works — I used the plant food once and my seed sprouted.' Ben says 'I planted 20 seeds with the food and 20 without, same everything else, and the food ones sprouted two days sooner on average.'
Decide whose evidence is stronger and explain why in terms of test design.
For each child, state the difference between the CLAIM ('the food makes seeds sprout faster') and the EVIDENCE (what was observed and how it was gathered).

Answer probing follow-ups: What did Ben compare against that Aisha didn't, and why does that matter? Does Aisha's sprouted seed prove the food worked, or could something else explain it? If Ben's food-seeds and no-food-seeds had sprouted at the same time, would that support or refute the claim?
activities.insight: Evidence is judged by its structure — a controlled comparison with multiple trials — not by whether it agrees with the claim or by who sounds more confident. A single confirming observation is not proof.

checkQuestion: Two children argue about whether a plant food makes seeds sprout faster. Aisha says, 'It works — I used it once and my seed sprouted.' Ben says, 'I planted 20 seeds with the food and 20 without, same everything else, and the food ones sprouted two days sooner on average.' Whose evidence is stronger, and why? What's the difference between their claim and their evidence?
checkAnswer: Ben's evidence is much stronger: he used a controlled comparison with many seeds (a fair test with multiple trials and a group without the food), so the difference can be attributed to the plant food. Aisha's is weak — a single observation with nothing to compare against; her seed might have sprouted anyway. A strong response separates the CLAIM ('the food makes seeds sprout faster') from the EVIDENCE (what was actually observed and how it was gathered), and judges evidence by control and number of trials.
